1.pericope_label: When Jabin king of Hazor had heard those things, he sent to the northern kings

schools.summary: Henry opens a second campaign and marks how it differs from the first: no less illustrious in success, but inferior in glory as to miracles, because the earlier wonders were meant to animate the people to act vigorously themselves. He turns that into a principle — the war carried on by the preaching of the gospel against Satan's kingdom was at first forwarded by miracles, but the war having been sufficiently proved to be of God, its managers are left to the ordinary assistance of grace, and must not expect hail-stones nor the standing still of the sun. On the confederacy Henry notes that the Canaanites were the aggressors, God hardening their hearts to begin the war so that Israel might be justified in destroying them; and he draws an uncomfortable comparison from their unity, since nations of divided interests combine here against Israel as against a common enemy — the children of this world being more unanimous, and therein wiser, than the children of light, so that the oneness of the church's enemies ought to shame the church's friends out of their discords.

Calvin reads the delay as providence. Had Jabin declared himself the ally of the neighbouring kings at the outset, a far more formidable war would have broken out; God could as easily have routed all their forces at once, but was unwilling to press beyond measure a people otherwise feeble, lest the sheer numbers of the enemy strike them with terror and drive them to despair. So he kept the many nations whose interest it was to rush to arms in a lethargy and amazement until the chosen people had been animated by signal victories — and their coming forward so late was the same as if they had entered into a truce, so that God not only fought for his people but, by dividing the enemy, increased their strength manifold, the earlier battles having only exercised them by pleasing preludes. Gill supplies what the northern king had heard — Jericho and Ai taken, the five kings defeated, the south subdued — and places Hazor on the lake Samachonitis, the same as the waters of Merom, adding that in Christ's time it was one of the ten cities of Decapolis.

Wesley arrives independently at Calvin's reading, calling it a remarkable instance of the wisdom of divine Providence, which so governed the minds of the Canaanites that they were not united under one king but divided among many petty ones, and that these did not join counsels at Israel's first entrance but quietly suffered the destruction of their brethren, thereby preparing the way for their own. Clarke suspects Jabin was not a personal name but the common name of the kings of Hazor, since the king who afterwards held Israel in slavery for twenty years bore it too; the word signifies wise, or intelligent. He sets Hazor above the Lake Semechon in Upper Galilee and notes that though Joshua burnt it the Canaanites rebuilt it, a powerful king reigning there some hundred and thirty years after Joshua's death; it was the metropolitan city of the district, with petty chieftains subject to it, which is why they were summoned now.

Ellicott places Jabin exactly: he was in northern Palestine what Adonizedek had been in the south, and the strength of that monarchy may be gathered from how formidable it proved when it recovered under the judges. He gives the modern identifications — Hazor as Jebel Hadirah near Kedes, Madon perhaps Madin west of the Sea of Galilee, Shimron as Simunieh west of Nazareth.

2.pericope_label: The kings of the north gathered, much people as the sand upon the sea shore, at the waters of Merom

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch trace the sweep of the alliance precisely — the mountains of Naphtali, the Arabah south of Chinnereth, that is the Ghor below the sea of Galilee, the northern lowland running down as far as Joppa, and the heights of Dor — and keep to the text on the numbers, a people as numerous as the sand by the sea-shore with very many horses and chariots. On Dor they add that it was built by Phoenicians who settled there for the abundance of purple mussels, lay below the promontory of Carmel some nine Roman miles north of Caesarea, and survives as a hamlet with considerable ruins; they locate the land of Mizpah below Hasbeya, where the village of Mutulleh, now inhabited by Druses, stands on a hill more than two hundred feet high commanding a splendid prospect over the Huleh basin — and it is from that prospect, they say, that the name derives. They identify Merom with Meirom, a celebrated place of Jewish pilgrimage two hours north-west of Szafed, where Hillel and Shammai are said to be buried. Ellicott equates Chinneroth with the Gennesaret of the New Testament, identifies Dor as Tantura and the land of Mizpeh with the plain El-Bukeia west of Hermon, and calls the waters of Merom the most northerly of the three lakes on the Jordan's course.

Clarke reports that Jerome and many since have taken Chinneroth for the town later called Tiberias, from which the lake probably took its name, and that Dor was the farthermost city of Phoenicia, in the lot of the half tribe of Manasseh. He lists four places called Mizpeh — in Judah, in Benjamin, beyond Jordan in Gad, and a fourth in Manasseh which he takes to be the one meant, following Calmet in supposing it where Laban and Jacob made their covenant. On the size of the host Clarke is sceptical: the comparison with sand conveys simply a number of which no regular estimate could be formed, and as for Josephus, who seldom finds difficulties in such cases and makes no scruple of speaking without book, he sets the allied armies at three hundred thousand foot, ten thousand horse and twenty thousand chariots. Clarke thinks the chariots the real point, since among the Canaanites they are generally supposed to have been armed with iron scythes fastened to the poles and wheel-naves, terrible things being told of the havoc they made among ranks of infantry — which is what Israel's armies wholly consisted of. Wesley reads the opening phrase as a general heading, all these places lying in the northern parts of Canaan as those of the previous chapter lay in the southern; he notes that Mizpeh signifies a watching-place and might therefore be applied to several places of good prospect, which is why there are so many, and describes Merom as a lake formed by the Jordan near Hazor, almost in the middle of the confederate kings.

Gill notes that Lebanon is the northern boundary and cites Josephus for the kings about Lebanon making war on Israel; on the muster he says only that the kings assembled at some certain place Jabin had appointed.

6.pericope_label: Be not afraid because of them: thou shalt hough their horses, and burn their chariots

schools.summary: Gill reports from Josephus that the multitude of the enemy terrified both Joshua and the Israelites, which is why the Lord appeared and spoke; but Gill himself thinks what was said was for the sake of the Israelites, who might well be disheartened, rather than for Joshua's, who was of a bold and courageous spirit — and he notes it cannot be settled whether the word came at Gilgal or later on the march. Calvin makes the encouragement proportional to the odds: the greater the labour and difficulty of destroying an army so numerous and well equipped, the more necessary to inspire fresh confidence. What he draws out of the repetition is the substance of the verse for him. God had promised Joshua success several times already, and as often as he reiterates his promises men are being reminded of their forgetfulness, or their sloth, or their fickleness; for unless new nourishment is given to faith every now and then, it faints and falls away — melts and vanishes, as his French has it. And yet such is our perverse fastidiousness that to hear the same thing twice is usually felt to be irksome. The lesson he wants is practical: as often as we are called to engage in new contests, let us recall the divine promises, which may correct our languor or rouse us from our sloth. Calvin then infers distance from the promise's wording — victory is pledged for the following day, so the enemy cannot have been far off, the lake of Merom lying contiguous to the Jordan and much nearer Gilgal than Gennesaret is.

Clarke will not draw Gill's distinction between Joshua and the people: to meet so formidable a host, well equipped and in its own country, required more than ordinary encouragement in Joshua's circumstances, and the communication was necessary to prevent the people from despairing on the eve of a conflict in which their all was at stake. Wesley explains the command as cutting the hamstrings, so that the animals should be unfit for war, and gives the reason at length: God had forbidden Israel to keep many horses, and now especially, so that they might not trust in their horses nor ascribe the conquest of the land to their own strength, but wholly to God — by whose power alone a company of raw and unexperienced footmen were able to subdue so potent a people, who besides their great numbers and their giants and their walled cities had the advantage of many thousands of horses and chariots.
Ellicott adds the one observation that answers the obvious objection to maiming animals: whatever is thought of the act, the command of Jehovah is the authority for it.

7.pericope_label: Joshua came against them suddenly; the LORD delivered them, and he houghed their horses

schools.summary: Clarke says Joshua, once apprised of the confederation, lost no time but marched to meet it, and fell upon the allies before they could have supposed him near. On the city they were chased to he enlarges with Homer, who praises Sidonian workmanship repeatedly — the embroidered robes that were no vulgar art, the silver urn excelled by none in weight or workmanship — and adds that Pliny credits the city with the invention of glass. On the maiming Clarke holds that the Hebrew word means to wound, cut or lop off, and very likely describes destroying the horses outright rather than merely disabling them, since God had purposed that his people should possess no such cattle at all, lest a warlike spirit be cultivated among them and they cease to depend on him — the same ground on which their kings were afterwards forbidden to multiply horses; the chariots were burnt because without the horses they could have been of no use. Wesley adds what the enemy were doing when the blow fell — they had gathered at Merom intending to refresh and order themselves for the offensive war they meant to wage — and reads the three directions of the pursuit together: the fugitives fled several ways, so the Israelites divided into two bodies, one pursuing east and the other west.

Gill suspects the force was not the whole body of armed men but a select company able to make quicker marches, and credits the timing to God, since it was of the Lord that Israel marched so fast and came upon them off their guard. Calvin infers the greatness of the overthrow from the distance, since the slaughter continued as far as Sidon, which lies far from the lake of Merom; he derives that city's epithet from its celebrity as a commercial emporium and the number of its inhabitants, and renders the second place-name the boiling of the waters, supposing thermal springs. But Calvin will not let the victory be explained by the ambush: the panic that hurried the allies into so scattered a flight shows they were driven headlong by the secret terror of the Lord, and the Israelites who dared follow through so many dangers were carried to a higher pitch of valour than is human by a celestial agency. His warmest praise is for what Joshua did afterwards, and it is praise for abstinence as much as prompt obedience — he would not have submitted so willingly to the loss of so many horses and chariots had not the fear of God overawed him, for such is our ingenuity in devising pretexts that it would have been perfectly plausible to argue that though the animals could not be fitted for military use, their value was by no means to be despised.

Ellicott notes that the surprise repeats the tactic of the campaign which began at Gibeon, Joshua surprising his adversaries by the rapidity of his movements; he identifies Misrephoth-maim with Zarephath, now Sarafend near Sidon. On the maiming he declines to settle what Clarke settles: in what way it was done we are not informed, and we cannot be certain whether it destroyed the animals' lives or merely made them useless for war. Keil and Delitzsch trace the rout north-west to Sidon, west as far as Misrephoth-maim and eastwards into the plain of Mizpah, and explain that Sidon is called great because it was then the metropolis of Phoenicia, though by David's day it had lost its splendour and been outstripped by its own daughter city Tyre; it survives as Saida.

10.pericope_label: Joshua turned back and took Hazor, and burnt it: for Hazor was the head of all those kingdoms

schools.summary: Gill explains the turning back: Joshua had chased the allies to Sidon and the other limits named, which carried him many miles past the city where he had first fallen upon them, so that taking Hazor meant retracing his steps — Bunting reckons it two and thirty miles from Sidon. Gill records what the taking included without softening it: all the souls that were in it, men, women and children.

Henry asks why the destruction of this one city is recorded so particularly, and answers that it was in Hazor, and by its king, that the whole daring design against Israel had been laid. He then follows the king's movements with some relish: the man escaped from the battle with his life and thought himself safe once back inside his own walls, Joshua having gone off in pursuit of the scattered troops in another direction — but it proved that what he took for his welfare was his trap, and there he was taken as in an evil net, slain in the place he had fled to, and his city burnt for his sake. Henry adds the sequel that complicates the record of a complete victory: the ruins were afterwards not well looked after by Israel, so that the Canaanites rebuilt the place and settled there again under another king of the same name — the Jabin who, generations later, oppressed Israel in the days of the judges.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the movement and what followed: after destroying the enemy and returning from the pursuit, Joshua took Hazor, smote its king and all its inhabitants with the sword, and burned the town, the former leader of all those kingdoms; and he dealt with the other towns exactly so, except that he did not burn them but left them standing upon their hills.
Wesley enters a limitation on the title given to Hazor: it was head not of all Canaan but of all those kingdoms confederate with it in this expedition.

12.pericope_label: The cities that stood still in their strength Israel burned not, save Hazor only

schools.summary: Gill names the towns that fell after Hazor was burnt — Madon, Shimron, Achshaph and the rest — and notes their kings were taken either there or earlier in the pursuit; on the disputed phrase he reports from Kimchi and Jarchi that it means cities whose walls were not demolished when they were taken, while allowing that it may mean they stood upon their heaps, on an eminence. On the spoil he lists what Israel took for itself — gold, silver, household goods, corn, wine, oil and merchandise, with cattle of every sort — and says plainly that this was allowed them. Calvin reads the campaign's method out of the exception: since the text says the cities which remained entire were not burned, it may be inferred with some probability that others were taken by force and assault and so razed, Hazor alone being destroyed by fire after the siege was over and the heat of the struggle had cooled, because it was the city which had held forth the torch that kindled the war. Calvin is watching the killing rather than the plunder, and insists that Joshua did not give loose rein to his passion when he slew all from the least to the greatest, but faithfully performed his part by fulfilling everything the Lord had enjoined through Moses — it is as if he had placed his hands at God's disposal. From which Calvin draws the principle that though the whole world should condemn us, it is enough to free us from all blame that we have the authority of God; adding at once the necessary guard, that it becomes us to consider prudently what each man's own vocation requires of him.

Clarke lays out two readings of the disputed phrase and prefers the topographical one on practical grounds — cities of the plain could be easily attacked and carried, so Joshua destroyed them, whereas those on hills and eminences could be held with little trouble, and prudence would dictate preserving them as places of refuge against any insurrection or invasion; he adds that this sense makes the prophet's promise that Jerusalem should be builded on her own heap read easily as a promise that she should be re-established on her own hill. The reading he reports but does not take is that the phrase means the cities which had made peace with Israel when terms were offered according to the law, and were consequently not destroyed, as the Hivite cities were not. On the spoil Clarke enters the one exception the law required: everything that had been employed for idolatrous purposes was withheld. Wesley glosses the phrase as with their fence, walls or bulwarks — those not ruined along with their walls in the taking — and gives Hazor's burning two motives: it began the war, and being the chief and royal city might renew it should the Canaanites ever seize it again, which he observes they did.

Ellicott renders the phrase literally as standing on their mounds, with the Vulgate behind him, but takes as his substantive judgement the reading Clarke declined: those who stood still in their strength are those who remained absolutely neutral in the war, and he contrasts them with Jericho and Ai, which he supposes committed themselves to hostile measures even though they were not able to send armies into the field before they were attacked.

15.pericope_label: He left nothing undone: Joshua took all that land, and made war a long time with all those kings

schools.summary: Henry treats the verse as the conclusion of the whole matter, and what strikes him is the Canaanites' obstinacy: though it appeared so manifestly that God fought for Israel, and though they had the worst of every engagement, they stood it out to the last, not one city making peace except Gibeon, who understood the things belonging to their peace better than their neighbours. Henry thinks the terms were there for the asking — the others might have made as good a bargain, and without ragged clothes and clouted shoes, had they humbled themselves; but they never so much as desired conditions of peace.

Clarke says the phrase about the mountain of Israel has given commentators much trouble, canvasses three solutions and prefers the first: that this verse and a later one were added after the kingdoms divided, there being in his view incontestable evidence that several notes were added to this book after Joshua's day. On the duration he does the arithmetic twice — Caleb was forty when sent from Kadesh-barnea and eighty-five at the war's end, which reckoning from the passage of Jordan gives exactly six years, the first spent on the south and the other five on the north, while Calmet gets seven from the same figures by subtracting both the forty and the thirty-eight wilderness years. Clarke supplies two further considerations on why the war was long, the first unexpectedly generous to the enemy: by protracting it the Canaanites had time to repent, having sufficient opportunity to discern the hand of Jehovah; the second is practical, that agriculture continued through those years, so provision was made even for the conquerors. Wesley gives five reasons of his own — lest the land become desert and the wild beasts multiply; lest a conquest done suddenly should be as quickly forgotten and despised, as human nature is apt to do; that by long exercise Israel might grow skilful in the art of war; for the trial of their patience and courage and trust in God; and to oblige them to greater care to please the God whose help they still needed.

Calvin rejects Clarke's premise about the mountain of Israel, holding it a mistake to suppose any particular mountain of that name is meant; the term is applied indiscriminately to the mountainous parts of both Israel and Judah, so that the passage sets up an antithesis, the hill country of the ten tribes being tacitly compared with that of Judah. On why the campaign was slow he denies it came from hesitation, weariness or sloth: the Lord was exercising his people variously, to give a brighter display of his manifold grace, which loses its value in our eyes if exhibited only in one and the same way — as the divine power had earlier been shown by the incredible ease with which five kingdoms fell almost at a run, so a lingering warfare now furnished numerous proofs of heavenly aid; and God had foretold through Moses that it would be so, lest the land, turned at once into a desert, be overrun by wild beasts. Gill reports that Josephus says five years, the common notion of the Jews seven, and Ussher six, concluding himself that it was six or seven.

Keil and Delitzsch judge the war as much as seven years from a later chapter, noting Josephus for five. Ellicott settles on seven and adds the comparison that makes the number meaningful: it is long when set beside the desultory incursions and single campaigns which made up most of ancient warfare, in an age with no standing armies.

19.pericope_label: It was of the LORD to harden their hearts, that they should come against Israel in battle

schools.summary: Calvin raises the difficulty that governs the passage, and raises it against himself. At first sight the statement contradicts what Moses says everywhere, that Israel was to enter into no league with these nations and make no terms of peace with them; and if the nations were thus excluded from the very means of making any compact, it seems absurd to ascribe their destruction to their own obstinacy. Suppose they had sent ambassadors ahead with olive branches, wholly intent on peace: Joshua must have answered that he could not lawfully negotiate, since the Lord had forbidden it. Had they made a hundred attempts to avoid war they must nevertheless have perished — so why are they blamed for not seeking peace, and is it not unjust to lay blame on men acting under compulsion? Calvin reports that the Greek translators appear to have felt the same pressure and evaded it, rendering the verse so that there was no city which Israel did not take, with the clause about peace removed altogether. Gill answers with a Jewish tradition that peace was genuinely available: on first landing, Joshua is said to have sent messages offering three courses — that those who wished to flee might flee, that those desirous of peace might make it, and that those for war might fight; all chose the last, and so perished. On the hardening Gill reaches for the obvious parallel, that God hardened these hearts as he had hardened Pharaoh's, so that his power might be displayed in their destruction.

Keil and Delitzsch shut Gill's door firmly: it cannot be inferred from this verse that if the Canaanites had received the Israelites amicably God would have withdrawn his command to destroy them and permitted Israel to make peace. They put the purpose in the plainest terms — God so ordered it that they hardened their heart to make war upon Israel, and thereby fell under the ban. Ellicott offers a correction and an argument: the word is better rendered as strengthening their heart, that is, rendering them obstinate; and these words go to prove, he says, what has been urged elsewhere — that the conquest of Canaan was not intended to be a massacre of unresisting inhabitants.

Clarke answers on different ground again, locating the guilt earlier than the war: they had sinned against all the light they had received, and God left them justly to the hardness, obstinacy and pride of their own hearts; since they chose to retain their idolatry he was determined they should be cut off, and their very refusal to make peace was the proof that they wilfully persisted in it. Wesley describes the hardening as a withholding rather than an infliction — it was the design of God's providence not to soften their hearts to a compliance with the Israelites, but to give them up to their own animosity, pride, confidence and stubbornness, so that their abominable and incorrigible wickedness might be punished, and that Israel might not be mixed with them but remain entire in possession of the land. He adds the practical consequence, that all who were taken were taken by the sword, so it is no wonder the war was long when the enemy was so obstinate.

21.pericope_label: Joshua cut off the Anakims: none were left, save in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod

schools.summary: Calvin explains why the Anakim get a paragraph of their own at the chapter's end. They were a race of giants, and it was the spies' account of their mighty stature that so terrified the people that they refused to enter Canaan at all; being objects of that much dread, it mattered greatly that they should be put out of the way and the people made more alert by good hopes of success. It would have been exceedingly injurious to keep permanently before their minds the very objects that filled them with alarm, since such fear obscured the glory due to God for former victories and overthrew their faith while they reflected that the hardest of all their contests was still to come. So the purging of the land of such monsters is rightly numbered among the instances of divine aid — and Calvin turns the terror into the argument: the less credible it seemed that they could be warred against with success, the more illustriously was the divine power displayed. Gill notes simply that those who escaped the sword fled elsewhere, to the places the text names.

Wesley uses this verse to answer the claim about the book's composition. That the mountains of Israel are named alongside those of Judah does not prove the book was written long after Joshua's death and after the kingdoms divided; at most it shows that this was a clause added later by Ezra or some other prophet, and Wesley thinks even that unnecessary — it was already evident to Joshua that Judah was to be chief of all the tribes, and some dawnings of its eminence appeared in his own time, in its having the first lot and the largest inheritance, so it is no wonder Judah should be mentioned apart. He then raises a harder question: how could Joshua be said to have utterly destroyed the Anakim, when Caleb and Othniel destroyed some of them after Joshua's death? Wesley offers two solutions and prefers the second — either these places, partly destroyed and then neglected, were repossessed by the giants and held until Caleb dislodged them, or, more likely, work actually done by Caleb's particular valour is ascribed to Joshua as general of the army. Clarke reads the passage structurally, as a recapitulation of operations already detailed in the previous chapter, notes that the cities destroyed were those of the Anakim since Joshua preserved certain others, and states the outcome precisely: the whole race was extirpated except those who took refuge in the Philistine cities, where descendants of Anak were still found as late as the days of David.

Ellicott makes the remnant concrete, suggesting that Goliath of Gath and his gigantic relatives seem to have been a part of it; he identifies Anab with the modern Anab, west of Debir, and observes that the deaths of Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai, the three sons of Anak, are recorded not here but in the book of Judges.

23.pericope_label: So Joshua took the whole land, and gave it for an inheritance; and the land rested from war

schools.summary: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown take the chapter's close as the place to face the doom pronounced on these nations. It cannot be reconciled with the divine character, they say, except on the assumption that the gross idolatry and enormous wickedness of the Canaanites left no reasonable hope of their repentance. If they were to be swept away as the antediluvians were, or the people of Sodom and Gomorrah, as incorrigible sinners who had filled up the measure of their iniquities, then it mattered nothing to them in what manner the judgment was inflicted; and God, as Sovereign Disposer, had a right to employ whatever instruments pleased him to execute it. They report a second defence without quite adopting it — that the Canaanites were unprincipled usurpers of a country God had assigned to the posterity of Eber, occupied ages earlier by wandering shepherds of that race, until the migration of Jacob's family into Egypt let the Canaanites overspread the land and hold it by force; on that view their expulsion was simply just. The standing prohibition against alliances they call a prudential rule founded on experience, that evil communications corrupt good manners — its necessity attested by the unhappy examples of Solomon and others later in the history.

Gill glosses the whole land as the far greater and better part, and points out what the sentence really asserts: of all he went against, Joshua failed in no attempt, and no place he besieged or summoned stood out. Calvin faces the apparent inaccuracy head on and resolves it by the clause that follows: although it was far from true that Joshua had actually acquired the whole land, he is truly said to have obtained it as God had declared to Moses, the second clause restricting the first, since it had been expressly added that the conquest would be made gradually, lest the land become a desert waste and Israel be left to war with the wild beasts of the woods. We are therefore at liberty to say that though the Lord had not yet put his people in possession, he had virtually performed what he agreed to do, in giving them a commodious habitation sufficient for the present. Calvin adds a further indication that districts not yet actually held are included: what they had acquired was distributed by families, and the distribution reached further than the possession.

Clarke follows the survivors out of the country. Besides the multitudes who perished, many took refuge in the confines of the land and among neighbouring nations; some suppose a party of them mastered Lower Egypt and founded the dynasty of the shepherd kings, though Clarke thinks those shepherds had occupied Egypt long before Jacob went down. He repeats a stranger tradition, that the fugitives founded Tangier, where Procopius reports two white pillars raised with an inscription in the Phoenician tongue: we are the persons who have fled from the face of Joshua the plunderer, the son of Nun. Many settled, he supposes, across Africa, Asia Minor, Greece and the islands, their descendants now so confounded with the nations as no longer to be discernible. On the closing act Clarke notes what Joshua did not take — no peculiar jurisdiction over the land, no peculiar share for his own family, and for himself only the ruined city of Timnath-serah, which he was obliged to rebuild. Wesley ends where the promise began: God had undertaken to drive out the nations, and now the undertaking was fulfilled; our successes and enjoyments are then doubly comfortable when we can see them flowing to us out of the promise, and if we make conscience of our duty we need not question the performance of it.
